questions.title: INNER JOIN vs. LEFT JOIN
questions.prompt: In SQL Server, what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN? Specifically, what happens to rows that don't have a match on the other side in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the ON condition evaluates true on both sides — any row from either table that has no match on the other side is dropped from the result entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in the FROM clause (the 'left' table), whether or not it has a match in the table named after JOIN (the 'right' table). When a left-table row has no match, every column that would have come from the right table comes back as NULL instead of the row being dropped. 'Left' and 'right' describe position in the query text — the table in FROM is left, the table after JOIN is right — not anything about the size or importance of the data. A common real use of LEFT JOIN is combining it with WHERE <right-table-column> IS NULL to find rows that have no match at all, since that column can only be NULL if the join failed to find a partner row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with a concrete example: if I join Product to SalesOrderDetail with an INNER JOIN, I only see products that have actually sold — a product sitting in inventory with zero orders just disappears from the result, because there's nothing on the right side to pair it with. If my actual question is 'show me every product, including the ones that have never sold,' INNER JOIN can't answer that by definition, so I switch to a LEFT JOIN from Product. Now every product shows up, and for the ones with no matching order, the order columns just come back NULL. That NULL is actually useful — if I add WHERE OrderQty IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN, I've just built a 'products that have never sold' report, which is a query I get asked for constantly in a reporting role. The one thing I'm careful to remember is that left and right only refer to where I physically wrote the table in the query, not which table is 'bigger' or more important.
questions.example:
-- INNER JOIN: only products with at least one order line
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- LEFT JOIN: every product, NULL-filled when there's no match
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- Finding products that have NEVER sold
SELECT p.Name
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID
WHERE sod.ProductID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Thinking 'left' and 'right' describe which table has more rows or matters more, instead of just position in the FROM/JOIN clause
Forgetting that unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL, then getting confused when COUNT() or SUM() on those columns behaves unexpectedly
Using INNER JOIN when the real goal is to find rows with no match — that specifically requires LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL check
Not realizing WHERE runs after the join, so a WHERE clause on a right-side column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into something that behaves like an INNER JOIN
keyPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in FROM, matched or not
Left/right refer to position in the query, not data meaning or size
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL in a LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the standard pattern for finding unmatched rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each join type returns
Explains NULL behavior for unmatched LEFT JOIN rows
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: WHERE vs. HAVING
questions.prompt: Why can't you filter on the result of an aggregate function (like AVG or COUNT) using a WHERE clause, and how does HAVING solve that problem? What is the correct logical order of FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and ORDER BY?
questions.modelAnswer: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY runs, so at the point WHERE executes, groups and their aggregated values (like AVG(ListPrice)) don't exist yet — there's nothing for WHERE to compare against. HAVING is WHERE's counterpart for groups: it runs after GROUP BY has formed the groups and after the aggregate functions have been computed, so by the time HAVING evaluates, every group's aggregate already exists and can be filtered on. The correct logical processing order in T-SQL is: FROM (and JOIN) first, then WHERE filters individual rows, then GROUP BY forms groups, then HAVING filters those groups, then SELECT picks the columns/expressions to return, and finally ORDER BY sorts the final result. WHERE and HAVING aren't mutually exclusive — you commonly use WHERE to remove rows before grouping even starts, and HAVING to filter the groups that result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as a timeline problem, not a syntax problem. If I write WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500, SQL Server throws an error, because logically WHERE runs before GROUP BY has even created any groups — there's no average to check yet. The moment I actually need to filter on an aggregated value, I move that condition to HAVING, which runs after the grouping and aggregation have already happened. In practice I use both together constantly: WHERE Color IS NOT NULL to throw out rows with no color recorded before I even start grouping, then GROUP BY Color, then HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500 to keep only the color groups whose average price clears that bar. I always come back to the same six-step order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — whenever I'm unsure why a query is or isn't behaving the way I expect.
questions.example:
SELECT Color, AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500;
-- WHERE removes NULL-color rows before grouping; HAVING keeps only
-- the color groups whose computed average price exceeds 500.
commonMistakes: Writing WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500 and being surprised by the error instead of recognizing aggregates aren't available yet at that stage
Assuming WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable, rather than realizing WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups
Not knowing the logical processing order, which makes debugging any non-trivial query much harder
Putting a filter that doesn't need aggregation into HAVING instead of WHERE, which is valid but wastes work filtering rows that could have been removed earlier
keyPoints: WHERE filters individual rows and runs before GROUP BY
HAVING filters groups and runs after GROUP BY and aggregation
Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
WHERE and HAVING can and often should be used together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why WHERE can't reference aggregates
Correctly states the logical processing order
Explains how WHERE and HAVING work together

questions.title: Primary keys vs. foreign keys
questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column, and what does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce between two tables? What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a foreign key?
questions.modelAnswer: A primary key guarantees two things at once about a column (or set of columns): every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL — together that means a primary key value always identifies exactly one row. Creating a primary key without specifying otherwise also builds a clustered index on it by default, physically sorting the table by that key. A foreign key enforces referential integrity: every value in the foreign-key column must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table. Trying to insert or update a row with a foreign-key value that doesn't exist in the referenced table fails with error 547 — the database physically refuses to create the orphaned row. ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default behavior (which blocks deleting a referenced row while dependents still point to it) so that deleting a parent row automatically deletes its dependent rows too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the primary key as the table's identity guarantee — Production.Product's primary key, ProductID, means I can always find exactly one product for a given ID, never zero, never two. The foreign key is what makes a JOIN trustworthy: Product.ProductSubcategoryID is a foreign key to ProductSubcategory, so SQL Server physically won't let me insert a product pointing at a subcategory that doesn't exist. If I try, I get error 547, which is the database doing its job, not a bug to work around. I'm careful with ON DELETE CASCADE, though — it's convenient for cleaning up dependent rows automatically, but on a deep relationship chain it can silently delete far more data than I expect, so I think through the blast radius before turning it on.
commonMistakes: Thinking a primary key only guarantees uniqueness and forgetting it also guarantees NOT NULL
Not realizing a primary key builds a clustered index by default unless you explicitly say NONCLUSTERED
Assuming a foreign key violation is just a warning rather than a hard failure (error 547) that blocks the write
Adding ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the deletion could cascade through a longer relationship chain
keyPoints: Primary key = unique + NOT NULL, identifying exactly one row
Primary key creates a clustered index by default
Foreign key enforces that a value must exist as a primary key in another table
Violating a foreign key raises Error 547
ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default block-on-delete behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a primary key guarantees
Correctly describes referential integrity and Error 547
Mentions the clustered index / cascade nuance

questions.title: CTEs vs. regular subqueries
questions.prompt: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE), and how does it differ from writing the same logic as a regular subquery? Why might you prefer a CTE?
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set defined at the top of a query with the WITH keyword. Functionally, it's equivalent to putting the same SELECT inside a subquery in the FROM clause — but instead of nesting it inline, you give it a name once and then reference that name like a real table in the statement that follows. This makes deeply nested subqueries much easier to read, especially when the same intermediate result needs to be referenced more than once in the outer query. A CTE is strictly temporary: it only exists for the single statement immediately following its WITH clause, is never saved anywhere, and disappears the moment that statement finishes — unlike a VIEW, which is a genuinely reusable, saved named query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I reach for a CTE mainly for readability. A subquery nested three levels deep inside a FROM clause gets hard to read fast — you end up mentally tracking which closing parenthesis belongs to which level. If I give that same logic a name with WITH CategoryAverages AS (...), I can read the outer query almost like English: 'from CategoryAverages, where...' That's especially valuable when I need to reference the same intermediate calculation more than once in the final query, since a CTE lets me do that without repeating the underlying SELECT. The one thing I always clarify for someone newer to this is that a CTE isn't a saved object — it only lives for the one statement right after it, so if I need that same logic reused across multiple separate queries, a VIEW is the right tool, not a CTE.
questions.example:
WITH CategoryAverages AS (
    SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID
)
SELECT ca1.ProductSubcategoryID, ca1.AvgPrice
FROM CategoryAverages AS ca1
WHERE ca1.AvgPrice > (SELECT AVG(AvgPrice) FROM CategoryAverages);
-- CategoryAverages is referenced twice in one statement -- hard to
-- do cleanly with a nested subquery instead.
commonMistakes: Thinking a CTE is saved/reusable across separate queries like a VIEW, rather than scoped to one statement
Not taking advantage of referencing the same CTE multiple times in the outer query
Assuming a CTE is always faster than a subquery -- it's primarily a readability tool, not automatically a performance one
Forgetting the WITH keyword needs to be the first word of the batch (or preceded by a semicolon) in some contexts
keyPoints: CTE = a named, temporary result set defined with WITH
Functionally equivalent to a FROM-clause subquery, but far more readable
Can be referenced multiple times in the statement that follows it
Scoped to one statement only -- not saved like a VIEW

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a CTE is
Explains the readability/multiple-reference advantage
Correctly notes the CTE is scoped to one statement, unlike a VIEW

questions.title: UNION vs. UNION ALL
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL when combining the result sets of two SELECT statements, and what two conditions must both SELECT statements satisfy before you can combine them at all?
questions.modelAnswer: UNION combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into one result set and removes any duplicate rows from that combined set, which requires SQL Server to do an implicit sort/distinct pass over the whole combined output. UNION ALL also combines the rows, but keeps every row exactly as returned, duplicates included, and skips the dedup pass entirely -- which makes it faster and cheaper to run whenever duplicates either can't occur or genuinely don't matter. Both statements being combined must return the same number of columns, and the data type in each corresponding column position must be compatible (not necessarily identical, but implicitly convertible) -- column names in the final result come from the first SELECT statement, regardless of what the second one used.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to UNION ALL unless I actually have a reason to expect duplicates and need them removed, because UNION ALL skips the sort/distinct work UNION does under the hood, so it's just cheaper to run on anything beyond a trivial row count. The two things I always check before combining two SELECTs this way: same number of columns on both sides, and compatible data types lining up column-by-column -- if the second SELECT's third column is a different, incompatible type from the first's third column, the combine fails outright. One detail that trips people up is that the final column names come entirely from the first SELECT -- aliasing a column differently in the second query doesn't change anything in the output.
questions.example:
-- UNION: removes duplicate rows across both queries
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';

-- UNION ALL: keeps every row, including duplicates, and skips the dedup work
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION ALL
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';
commonMistakes: Using UNION by default everywhere, paying for a dedup pass that isn't actually needed
Assuming the two SELECTs need identical column names instead of just a matching column count and compatible types
Not realizing the final result's column names come from the first SELECT, regardless of aliases used in the second
Forgetting ORDER BY can only appear once, at the very end of the combined statement, not after each individual SELECT
keyPoints: UNION removes duplicate rows across the combined result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row
UNION ALL is cheaper -- it skips the sort/distinct pass UNION performs
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible data types per position
Result column names come from the first SELECT statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the duplicate-removal difference
Correctly states the column-count/data-type compatibility requirement
Mentions the performance implication of the dedup pass

questions.title: DTU vs. vCore, at a glance
questions.prompt: At a high level, what's the difference between the DTU-based and vCore-based purchasing models for Azure SQL Database, and why might a DBA prefer vCore even for a small database?
questions.modelAnswer: The DTU (Database Transaction Unit) model bundles compute, memory, and I/O into a single blended unit -- simple to pick a tier, but opaque, since a DTU percentage alone doesn't tell you which specific resource is actually the bottleneck. The vCore model instead lets you choose compute and storage independently, with compute mapped directly to a number of virtual cores, which is both easier to reason about and easier to compare against an on-prem server's core count. A DBA might prefer vCore even for a small database because vCore is required to use Azure Hybrid Benefit (applying an existing SQL Server license for a licensing discount), and because vCore unlocks tiers DTU doesn't offer at all, like serverless (auto-pause/auto-scale compute) and Hyperscale (for databases that may need to grow far beyond a typical size later).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame DTU as the simpler but blurrier option -- one slider, one number, but when something's slow I can't easily tell from DTU percentage alone whether it's actually CPU, memory, or I/O that's maxed out. vCore separates those out, lets me size compute and storage independently, and maps compute to actual vCore counts, which also happens to make it much easier to have an apples-to-apples conversation with someone used to on-prem core-based licensing. The concrete reason I'd pick vCore even for something small is Azure Hybrid Benefit -- if the company already owns SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance, that discount is only available under vCore, not DTU -- plus vCore is the only path to serverless compute, which can be genuinely cheaper for a small, intermittently-used database that doesn't need to run at full capacity around the clock.
commonMistakes: Assuming DTU is simpler to monitor, when it's actually harder to isolate which specific resource is the bottleneck
Not knowing Azure Hybrid Benefit only applies under the vCore model
Assuming a small database must default to DTU, missing serverless as a vCore-only, cost-efficient option for light workloads
Treating the two models as equivalent in capability rather than vCore offering tiers (Hyperscale, serverless) DTU doesn't have
keyPoints: DTU bundles compute, memory, and I/O into one blended unit
vCore lets compute and storage be sized independently, mapped to actual core counts
Azure Hybrid Benefit licensing savings require the vCore model
vCore unlocks serverless and Hyperscale tiers that DTU doesn't offer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the DTU vs. vCore distinction
Gives a concrete reason to prefer vCore
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What installing and configuring SQL Server actually involves
questions.prompt: At a glance, what are the main decisions a DBA has to make when installing and initially configuring an on-prem SQL Server instance, beyond just clicking 'Next' through the setup wizard?
questions.modelAnswer: Installation planning happens before the installer ever runs: choosing the edition (Standard vs. Enterprise, since that affects both cost and which features are even available), picking the service accounts SQL Server and SQL Server Agent will run as (ideally dedicated, least-privilege domain or managed service accounts, not a personal admin login), and deciding the collation up front, since changing a server's collation after the fact is disruptive and sometimes requires rebuilding system databases. During setup, the DBA chooses the authentication mode (Windows Authentication only, or Mixed Mode to also allow SQL logins) and sets the initial sa password if Mixed Mode is enabled. After install, post-install configuration covers things the wizard doesn't fully handle: setting max server memory so SQL Server doesn't starve the OS of RAM, configuring tempdb with multiple data files sized appropriately for the expected workload, and reviewing server-level settings like max degree of parallelism (MAXDOP) and cost threshold for parallelism. None of this is optional busywork -- a default, unconfigured instance can genuinely cause production problems like memory pressure or tempdb contention later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as three stages. Before I even launch the installer, I decide on the edition, pick dedicated service accounts rather than reusing someone's personal login, and lock in the collation, since that's painful to change later. During the actual setup wizard, the two choices that matter most are the authentication mode -- Windows-only or Mixed Mode -- and, if Mixed Mode is on, setting a genuinely strong sa password immediately rather than leaving it default. The part that's easy to skip but shouldn't be is everything after setup finishes: I always set max server memory explicitly, because an unconfigured instance will happily consume all the RAM on the box and starve the OS; I configure tempdb with multiple equally-sized data files instead of leaving it as the single small default file; and I check MAXDOP and cost threshold for parallelism against the box's actual core count rather than trusting the out-of-the-box defaults, which are tuned for a much smaller server than most production hardware today.
commonMistakes: Treating the setup wizard as the entire installation process and skipping post-install configuration entirely
Leaving max server memory unset, letting SQL Server consume all available RAM and starve the OS
Leaving tempdb as a single small default data file instead of sizing and splitting it for the workload
Picking the collation casually, not realizing how disruptive it is to change later
keyPoints: Pre-install decisions: edition, service accounts, collation
During setup: authentication mode and the sa password (if Mixed Mode)
Post-install: max server memory, tempdb sizing, MAXDOP/cost threshold for parallelism
Defaults are not production-ready out of the box

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies pre-install decisions (edition, accounts, collation)
Correctly identifies key post-install configuration steps
Explains why defaults aren't sufficient for production

questions.title: Basic DMVs every DBA checks first
questions.prompt: What is a DMV (Dynamic Management View), and which two or three would you check first if someone reported 'the server feels slow right now'?
questions.modelAnswer: A DMV is a system view that exposes SQL Server's own internal, real-time state -- sessions, queries currently running, locks held, memory and I/O usage -- queryable with ordinary SELECT statements rather than requiring a separate monitoring tool. For a live 'it feels slow' report, the first checks are sys.dm_exec_requests, which shows every currently executing request along with its wait_type and blocking_session_id, immediately revealing whether sessions are actively waiting on something and on what; sys.dm_exec_sessions, which shows who is connected and from where; and sys.dm_os_wait_stats, which shows the cumulative time SQL Server has spent waiting on each wait type since the last restart, useful for spotting a systemic pattern rather than just one moment in time. Together, dm_exec_requests answers 'what's happening right now,' and dm_os_wait_stats answers 'what's SQL Server generally been waiting on.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go to sys.dm_exec_requests first, because it shows me every request actually running at this exact moment, along with its wait_type and whether blocking_session_id points at another session -- that single query usually tells me in seconds whether something is actively blocked, and by whom. I'd pair that with sys.dm_exec_sessions to see who's connected and from where, in case it's one runaway connection rather than a general slowdown. If nothing jumps out live, I'd check sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the server's cumulative wait profile since the last restart, which tells me the kind of resource SQL Server has generally been starved for -- CPU, I/O, locking -- over time rather than just this one moment. I wouldn't reach for a third-party tool before checking these, since they're built into SQL Server and answer the first, most urgent question immediately.
questions.example:
-- What's running right now, and is anything blocked?
SELECT session_id, status, wait_type, wait_time, blocking_session_id, command
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE session_id > 50;

-- Cumulative wait profile since the last restart
SELECT TOP 10 wait_type, wait_time_ms, waiting_tasks_count
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
commonMistakes: Not knowing DMVs are built-in, queryable system views rather than requiring a separate monitoring product
Jumping straight to restarting the instance or a service before checking what's actually running
Confusing a live snapshot (dm_exec_requests) with cumulative history (dm_os_wait_stats) and drawing the wrong conclusion
Filtering out session_id <= 50 by habit without knowing that excludes SQL Server's own internal system sessions
keyPoints: A DMV is a built-in system view exposing SQL Server's live internal state
sys.dm_exec_requests shows what's running right now, including wait_type and blocking_session_id
sys.dm_exec_sessions shows who's connected and from where
sys.dm_os_wait_stats shows the cumulative wait profile since the last restart

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a DMV is
Names appropriate DMVs for a live slowness report
Explains what each chosen DMV reveals

questions.title: Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL at a glance, for a SQL Server DBA
questions.prompt: If you already know SQL Server well, what's the quick mental model for how Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL differ from it and from each other, at a glance?
questions.modelAnswer: Oracle is the closest to SQL Server in terms of being a single, comprehensive, enterprise-grade relational engine, but its core terminology maps differently -- what SQL Server calls an 'instance' containing many 'databases' is closer to an Oracle 'instance' paired with a single 'database' made up of tablespaces, and Oracle's backup/recovery tool, RMAN, and its SQL*Plus/SQL Developer client tools are different enough from SSMS to need dedicated study. MySQL is historically a lighter-weight engine, commonly chosen for web applications, with a notable architectural quirk -- it supports multiple interchangeable storage engines (InnoDB being the modern default) underneath one SQL layer, which affects things like transaction support and locking behavior depending on which engine a table actually uses. PostgreSQL sits philosophically closest to a 'do it correctly, extensibly, and by the SQL standard' design, with a strong reputation for advanced data types and extensibility, and configuration that leans more on text configuration files (postgresql.conf, pg_hba.conf) than a GUI. All three remain relational and SQL-based at their core, so joins, keys, and transactions transfer conceptually -- what doesn't transfer directly is the tooling, the exact SQL dialect, and platform-specific behaviors like Oracle's lack of autocommit by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give a one-line anchor for each. Oracle feels the most like 'enterprise SQL Server, but with different nouns and its own backup tool' -- the concepts (instances, tablespaces, users/schemas) are recognizable, but the tools are completely different, and RMAN is not something I can bluff through just because I know BACKUP DATABASE. MySQL I think of as 'lighter and web-oriented, with a storage-engine twist' -- the fact that a single MySQL server can have tables using different storage engines underneath one SQL layer is genuinely a different mental model than SQL Server, where the storage engine isn't something you choose per table. PostgreSQL I think of as 'the standards-purist, config-file-driven option' -- it's taken seriously for correctness and extensibility, but a lot of what I'd configure through SSMS dialogs on SQL Server, I'm editing directly in postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf text files on Postgres. What stays constant across all three and SQL Server is that they're relational -- SELECT, JOIN, and ACID transactions are still the mental model -- the differences are in tooling, dialect, and specific defaults.
commonMistakes: Assuming all relational databases work close enough to SQL Server that nothing new needs to be learned
Not knowing MySQL supports multiple storage engines per table under one SQL layer
Expecting Oracle's backup/recovery tooling (RMAN) to resemble SQL Server's BACKUP/RESTORE statements
Not realizing PostgreSQL configuration leans heavily on text files rather than a GUI
keyPoints: Oracle: closest in scale/enterprise feel, but different terminology and tooling (RMAN, SQL*Plus)
MySQL: lighter, web-oriented, with interchangeable storage engines per table
PostgreSQL: standards-focused and extensible, configured mainly through text files
All three stay relational/SQL-based conceptually; tooling and dialect are what genuinely differ

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives an accurate, distinguishing one-line mental model for each platform
Correctly identifies what transfers (relational concepts) vs. what doesn't (tooling/dialect)
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What MongoDB and document databases are, at a glance
questions.prompt: For someone who only knows relational databases like SQL Server, what is a document database like MongoDB, at a glance, and how does storing data in it differ from storing it in tables and rows?
questions.modelAnswer: A document database stores data as self-contained documents -- in MongoDB's case, BSON (a binary form of JSON) -- grouped into collections, which are the loose equivalent of tables, except a collection doesn't enforce a single fixed schema the way a SQL Server table does; different documents in the same collection can have different fields. Where a relational design normalizes related data into separate tables joined by foreign keys (a Customer table, an Order table, an OrderLine table), a document database commonly embeds related data directly inside a single document -- an order document might contain its line items as a nested array right inside it, rather than requiring a join to assemble them at query time. This trades the strict structure and join-based flexibility of a relational model for a model that's often faster to read in one round trip, because the related data travels together, but which requires a deliberate design decision up front -- embed or reference -- rather than SQL Server's default of always normalizing and joining.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as the data living together instead of being split apart and joined back together at query time. In SQL Server, an order and its line items live in two separate, normalized tables, and I join them to see the full picture. In MongoDB, I'd commonly store that whole order, including its line items, as one JSON-like document, so reading it back is often a single lookup instead of a join across tables. Collections are MongoDB's rough equivalent of tables, but they don't enforce one rigid schema -- two documents in the same collection can genuinely have different fields, which would be unusual for two rows in the same SQL Server table. The real design shift for someone coming from SQL Server is that 'should this be embedded in the parent document, or kept as its own separate, referenced document' becomes a deliberate modeling decision, instead of normalization just being the default, assumed answer the way it is in a relational schema.
commonMistakes: Assuming a MongoDB collection enforces the same fixed schema a SQL Server table does
Treating 'document database' as just 'a table that stores JSON' without grasping the embed-vs-reference design shift
Expecting joins to work the same way they do in SQL Server rather than recognizing related data is often embedded instead
Not recognizing that schema flexibility is a deliberate trade-off, not simply 'less structured and therefore worse'
keyPoints: A document database stores self-contained documents (BSON/JSON) grouped into collections
Collections don't enforce one fixed schema across all documents, unlike a SQL Server table
Related data is commonly embedded directly in a document instead of normalized across separate joined tables
Embed-vs-reference is a deliberate design decision, replacing the relational default of always normalizing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes documents/collections at a basic level
Correctly contrasts embedding with relational normalization/joins
Clarity of explanation for a relational-background audience

questions.title: Write a GROUP BY aggregate query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns each distinct Color along with the count of products of that color and the average ListPrice for that color, excluding rows where Color is NULL.
questions.code:
-- Production.Product (AdventureWorks2012) has columns including:
-- ProductID, Name, Color, ListPrice
USE AdventureWorks2012;
GO
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY works in three conceptual steps: split the table into groups (one group per distinct Color value), aggregate within each group separately (COUNT and AVG each run once per group, not once overall), then combine the results into one row per group. Every column in SELECT must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or listed in GROUP BY — Color qualifies because it's the GROUP BY column; Name would not be allowed unaggregated here because it varies within a color group. Filtering out NULL colors belongs in WHERE, since that's a row-level filter that should happen before grouping, not a group-level filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write WHERE Color IS NOT NULL first, since that's just removing rows before grouping even starts — no reason to let NULL colors form their own group if the business doesn't care about them. Then GROUP BY Color splits the remaining rows into one bucket per color, and COUNT(*) plus AVG(ListPrice) each compute their own answer per bucket rather than one answer for the whole table. The result has exactly one row per distinct color — the same number of rows COUNT(DISTINCT Color) would report — which is a good sanity check I'd run after writing a query like this.
questions.example:
SELECT Color,
       COUNT(*) AS ProductCount,
       AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
ORDER BY ProductCount DESC;
-- One row per distinct Color; COUNT and AVG are computed per color group.
commonMistakes: Adding Name or another non-aggregated, non-grouped column to SELECT and getting a GROUP BY error
Filtering NULL colors with HAVING instead of WHERE, doing unnecessary work by grouping rows that should have been excluded first
Forgetting WHERE Color IS NOT NULL entirely and getting an extra group for NULL
Confusing COUNT(*) (counts rows) with COUNT(Color) (counts non-NULL Color values) when NULLs are still present
keyPoints: GROUP BY splits rows into groups, aggregates within each, then combines into one row per group
Every SELECT column must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY
Row-level filters (like excluding NULL) belong in WHERE, before grouping
Result row count should match COUNT(DISTINCT <grouped column>)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GROUP BY syntax and aggregate functions
Correctly excludes NULL colors with WHERE, not HAVING
Explains why the query is structured that way

questions.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side
questions.prompt: Write a query that ranks products by ListPrice descending using ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in the same result set, and explain how the three functions differ when two products are tied for the same price.
questions.modelAnswer: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique, sequential numbers — even for genuinely tied values, it arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives one row a lower number than the other. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but leaves a gap afterward: if two products tie for rank 1, the next distinct price gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() accounts for how many rows were tied at the previous rank. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but with no gap — the next distinct price after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2. All three are computed with an OVER (ORDER BY ...) window clause and require no GROUP BY.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run all three in one query so the difference is visible directly in the output rather than just described. If two products are tied for the most expensive, ROW_NUMBER() pretends there's no tie at all and numbers them 1 and 2 arbitrarily — which would misrepresent a genuine tie as a win. RANK() is honest about the tie: both get rank 1, but the next product jumps to rank 3, because two rows already occupied rank 1's 'slot.' DENSE_RANK() is also honest about the tie — both get rank 1 — but it only cares about distinct values, so the next price tier is rank 2 with no gap. Which one I pick depends on the business question: a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for second place genuinely skips third place calls for RANK(); a scale of distinct price tiers where I just want the next gap-free tier number calls for DENSE_RANK().
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- Tied prices: RowNum stays unique, Rank_ ties then skips ahead,
-- DenseRank_ ties with no gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming ROW_NUMBER() is 'safer' for ties when it actually hides them by assigning arbitrary unique numbers
Confusing RANK's gap-after-a-tie behavior with DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Forgetting that ORDER BY inside OVER() determines which rows get which rank — changing it changes the whole result
Trying to use these functions without an OVER() clause, or expecting them to need a GROUP BY
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, even for ties
RANK() ties share a number but the next value skips ahead by the tie size
DENSE_RANK() ties share a number with no gap for the next distinct value
All three run inside OVER (ORDER BY ...), no GROUP BY needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct syntax for all three ranking functions
Accurately explains the tie-handling difference
Picks a sensible real-world scenario for each function

questions.title: Write a parameterized stored procedure
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure named usp_GetProductsAbovePrice that accepts a @MinPrice parameter defaulting to 100, and returns the Name and ListPrice of every product in Production.Product with a ListPrice at or above that value, ordered by price descending. Then show how you'd call it both with and without supplying a value for @MinPrice.
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter is declared right after the procedure name, before the AS keyword, and behaves like a normal variable throughout the procedure body — it's just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in. Giving a parameter a default value (@MinPrice MONEY = 100) makes it optional: if the caller doesn't supply a value, SQL Server uses the default automatically. Calling the procedure with named notation (EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500) is unambiguous and order-independent, which is why it's preferred over positional calling once a procedure has more than one parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the parameter with a sensible default so the procedure is usable both ways out of the box. The body itself is just the same filtered, sorted SELECT I'd write ad hoc, except @MinPrice stands in for whatever literal value I'd otherwise hard-code. Calling it with EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice; uses the default of 100 automatically, and calling it with @MinPrice = 500 overrides that for just this call. I always call with named parameters -- @MinPrice = 500 instead of just 500 -- because the moment a procedure picks up a second or third parameter, positional calling becomes an easy way to silently pass values to the wrong parameter.
questions.example:
CREATE PROCEDURE usp_GetProductsAbovePrice
    @MinPrice MONEY = 100
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT Name, ListPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    WHERE ListPrice >= @MinPrice
    ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500; -- overrides the default
EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice;                 -- uses the default, 100
commonMistakes: Forgetting the default value, which forces every caller to always supply @MinPrice even when a sensible default exists
Calling the procedure positionally once it has multiple parameters, risking values landing in the wrong parameter
Putting the parameter declaration after AS instead of before it
Hard-coding the price threshold inside the procedure body instead of parameterizing it, defeating the point of a reusable procedure
keyPoints: Parameters are declared before AS and behave like pre-populated variables
A default value makes a parameter optional
Named notation (@Param = value) is unambiguous and order-independent
EXEC without a value for an optional parameter falls back to its default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE PROCEDURE syntax with a default parameter
Correct query logic (filter + sort)
Shows both calling styles (with and without override)

questions.title: Write a full database backup statement
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL statement that takes a full backup of a database named SalesDB to a local disk path, and explain the difference between a full backup and a transaction log backup in terms of what each one actually captures.
questions.code: -- Goal: BACKUP DATABASE SalesDB TO DISK = '...' WITH options
questions.modelAnswer: BACKUP DATABASE <name> TO DISK = '<path>.bak' WITH <options> captures every data page needed to reconstruct the entire database as of the moment the backup finishes, including the transactional detail needed to bring it to a consistent state. A transaction log backup instead captures only the log records written since the last log backup (or since the full backup, for the very first one) — a much smaller, incremental slice — which is what makes point-in-time restore between full backups possible. Log backups are only meaningful under the FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery model; under SIMPLE, the log is truncated automatically and log backups aren't part of the strategy at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write BACKUP DATABASE SalesDB TO DISK = 'C:\Backups\SalesDB_Full.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM, and I'd always default to adding COMPRESSION and CHECKSUM as good practice, not just the bare minimum syntax. The distinction I'd make sure to get right: a full backup is a complete snapshot of every data page as of the moment it finishes, while a log backup only grabs the transaction log records written since the last log backup — a much smaller, incremental slice that's what actually lets me restore to a specific point in time between full backups. And I'd flag that log backups only make sense at all under the FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery model; a database sitting in SIMPLE recovery is truncating its log automatically, so there's nothing meaningful to back up that way.
commonMistakes: Forgetting a database in SIMPLE recovery model can't take meaningful transaction log backups
Assuming a full backup only captures data as of when it started, rather than being consistent as of when it finishes
Not adding WITH CHECKSUM/COMPRESSION as standard practice
Confusing a differential backup (changes since the last full) with a transaction log backup (all log records since the last log backup)
keyPoints: BACKUP DATABASE ... TO DISK is the basic full-backup syntax
A full backup is a complete, consistent copy of all data pages as of completion
A log backup captures only log records since the last log backup, enabling point-in-time restore
The recovery model (FULL/BULK_LOGGED vs. SIMPLE) governs whether log backups are meaningful

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct BACKUP DATABASE syntax
Correctly distinguishes full vs. log backup content
Mentions the recovery model dependency

questions.title: Write a basic nonclustered index
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL statement that creates a nonclustered index on the OrderDate column of a Sales.Orders table, and explain at a high level why an index on a frequently-filtered column speeds up a query.
questions.code: -- Goal: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ... ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate)
questions.modelAnswer: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate); builds a separate, smaller structure that's sorted by OrderDate and holds a pointer back to each full row. A query that filters on OrderDate can then seek directly to the matching range inside that small sorted structure instead of scanning every row in the table just to check each one's OrderDate — that's the practical difference between an index seek and a full table scan, and it's the reason the same query can go from checking every row to checking only the handful that actually match.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate); and explain it as giving SQL Server a shortcut: instead of reading the whole table row by row to find which ones fall in a given date range, it can jump straight into this much smaller, OrderDate-sorted structure, find the matching range, and use the pointers stored there to go get just those specific rows. That's an index seek instead of a table scan, and on a large table that difference can be the entire performance story for a query. I'd also be upfront that this isn't free — every index adds overhead to every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches OrderDate, so it's a tradeoff, not a universal win.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate
ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate);
commonMistakes: Assuming every column should be indexed, ignoring the write-cost an index adds
Forgetting a nonclustered index is a separate structure, not a physical reordering of the table itself (only the clustered index does that)
Expecting an index to help a query that doesn't actually filter or sort on an indexed column
Not giving the index a meaningful, identifiable name
keyPoints: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX syntax targets a specific column
An index is a separate, smaller sorted structure plus a pointer back to the full row
It enables an index seek instead of a full table scan on a filtered query
Indexes have a write-cost on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches the indexed column

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX syntax
Correctly explains seek vs. scan
Mentions the write-cost tradeoff

questions.title: Write the T-SQL to create a basic SQL Server Agent job
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL (using the msdb system stored procedures) to create a SQL Server Agent job called 'Nightly Index Maintenance' with one step that runs EXEC dbo.usp_IndexMaintenance, and a daily schedule that runs it at 1:00 AM.
questions.code:
-- Goal: sp_add_job, sp_add_jobstep, sp_add_schedule, sp_attach_schedule,
-- sp_add_jobserver, all in the msdb database
questions.modelAnswer: A SQL Server Agent job is really four related pieces, each created with its own msdb stored procedure: sp_add_job creates the job itself (just a name and a few metadata settings, no steps yet); sp_add_jobstep adds one step to that job, specifying the actual command to run and which subsystem runs it (TSQL for a plain T-SQL command); sp_add_schedule creates a reusable schedule definition (daily, at a specific time); and sp_attach_schedule links that schedule to the job. Finally, sp_add_jobserver tells the job which server (local, by default) is actually responsible for running it -- a step that's easy to forget, and without it the job exists but never actually executes anywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build it in the order SQL Server actually expects: first sp_add_job to create the shell of the job with just a name, then sp_add_jobstep to attach the one step that runs EXEC dbo.usp_IndexMaintenance with @subsystem = 'TSQL'. Then I'd create the schedule separately with sp_add_schedule, specifying @freq_type = 4 for daily and @active_start_time = 010000 for 1 AM, and attach it to the job with sp_attach_schedule. The step people most often forget is sp_add_jobserver -- without explicitly telling SQL Server which server runs this job (@server_name = N'(local)' in a single-instance setup), the job gets created but never actually gets scheduled to run anywhere, which is a confusing, silent gap to debug later.
commonMistakes: Forgetting sp_add_jobserver, leaving a fully configured job that never actually runs anywhere
Not specifying @database_name on the jobstep, causing the step to run against the wrong database context
Getting @freq_type/@freq_interval wrong and scheduling something weekly or monthly by accident instead of daily
Creating the job and step but never creating or attaching a schedule at all, leaving it to only run manually
keyPoints: sp_add_job creates the job shell; sp_add_jobstep adds the actual command and subsystem
sp_add_schedule defines a reusable schedule; sp_attach_schedule links it to a specific job
sp_add_jobserver assigns which server runs the job -- easy to forget, breaks execution silently
The TSQL subsystem runs a plain T-SQL command as the step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct sp_add_job and sp_add_jobstep usage
Correct sp_add_schedule/sp_attach_schedule usage for a daily 1 AM schedule
Includes sp_add_jobserver and explains why it's needed

questions.title: Write basic index and statistics maintenance T-SQL
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks the average fragmentation of indexes on a table using sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats, then shows the appropriate maintenance command for a case where fragmentation is moderate (10-30%) versus severe (over 30%).
questions.code: -- Goal: query sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats, then ALTER INDEX REORGANIZE vs REBUILD
questions.modelAnswer: A maintenance plan is, conceptually, just a scheduled bundle of these same routine upkeep tasks -- index maintenance, statistics updates, integrity checks, backups -- run on a schedule via SQL Server Agent, whether built through the SSMS wizard or scripted directly in T-SQL. sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats returns avg_fragmentation_in_percent for each index, which is the number that decides the action: between roughly 10% and 30% fragmented, SQL Server's own guidance is to reorganize (ALTER INDEX ... REORGANIZE), which is an online, lower-impact operation that tidies pages in place; above roughly 30%, reorganizing isn't enough, and the guidance shifts to rebuilding (ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD), which fully recreates the index and also refreshes its statistics as a side effect.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by actually measuring instead of maintaining on a guess -- sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats gives me avg_fragmentation_in_percent per index, and that number is what drives the decision, not a fixed schedule applied blindly to every index. Between 10% and 30%, I reorganize, since that's a lighter, fully online operation that just shuffles pages back into order without taking a bigger lock. Past 30%, reorganizing stops being worth it and I rebuild instead, which fully recreates the index and also freshens its statistics along the way. In practice, on a production system, I wouldn't hand-write this fragmentation check and branching logic myself from scratch -- I'd use Ola Hallengren's maintenance scripts, which already encode exactly this reorganize-vs-rebuild threshold logic and are the de facto industry standard -- but I'd still want to be able to explain and reproduce the underlying logic by hand, which is what this query does.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding every index on a fixed schedule regardless of actual fragmentation, wasting resources on indexes that didn't need it
Using REORGANIZE on severely fragmented indexes when a REBUILD is what's actually needed
Not knowing a REBUILD also refreshes statistics as a side effect, and separately scheduling a redundant stats update right after
Hand-rolling this logic in production instead of using (or at least knowing about) Ola Hallengren's widely-adopted maintenance scripts
keyPoints: A maintenance plan is a scheduled bundle of index/stats/integrity/backup tasks run via SQL Server Agent
sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats reports avg_fragmentation_in_percent per index
10-30% fragmented: REORGANIZE (lighter, online); over 30%: REBUILD (heavier, also refreshes statistics)
Ola Hallengren's scripts are the industry-standard way to automate this logic in production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly queries sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats
Correctly applies the reorganize-vs-rebuild threshold
Mentions Ola Hallengren's scripts as the production-standard approach

questions.title: Reading a basic actual execution plan
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL to turn on the actual execution plan for a simple SELECT with a WHERE clause, and explain the two or three things a beginner should look at first in the resulting plan to judge whether the query is running efficiently.
questions.code:
-- Goal: SET STATISTICS XML ON (or SSMS 'Include Actual Execution Plan'),
-- then interpret Scan vs Seek and the thickness of arrows
questions.modelAnswer: Turning on SET STATISTICS XML ON before running a query (or clicking 'Include Actual Execution Plan' in SSMS) captures the real plan SQL Server used, including the actual number of rows that flowed through each step -- as opposed to the estimated plan, which shows what the optimizer expected before running anything. For a beginner reading the resulting plan, three things matter most at a glance: first, whether the access to the main table is a Seek or a Scan -- a Seek means an index was used to jump straight to matching rows, a Scan means every row was read and checked, which is often (not always) a red flag on a large table; second, the relative cost percentage shown under each operator, since that points to which part of the plan is actually expensive rather than guessing; and third, a large gap between estimated and actual row counts on any operator, which signals the optimizer's assumptions were wrong and the plan it chose may not actually be a good one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd turn on the actual plan with SET STATISTICS XML ON, or just click the 'Include Actual Execution Plan' button in SSMS before running the query, since the actual plan shows real row counts, not the optimizer's guesses. The first thing I look at is the rightmost operators, where data access starts -- is it a Seek, meaning an index got used to jump to the right rows, or a Scan, meaning it read every row in the table or index to find them. A Scan isn't automatically wrong on a small table, but on a large one it's usually the first thing worth questioning. Second, I look at the cost percentage SSMS shows under each operator, which tells me where the expensive part of the plan actually is instead of guessing. Third, I compare the estimated and actual row counts on a few key operators -- a big mismatch there tells me the optimizer's assumptions were off, which often explains a plan that looks fine on paper but performs badly in reality.
commonMistakes: Reading the estimated plan instead of the actual plan, missing real row-count information
Treating every Scan as automatically bad, without considering table size or whether a Seek would even help
Not checking the per-operator cost percentage, and instead guessing at which part of the query is slow
Ignoring a large estimated-vs-actual row count mismatch, which is often the real root cause of a bad plan
keyPoints: SET STATISTICS XML ON (or Include Actual Execution Plan) captures the real, executed plan with actual row counts
Seek vs. Scan on the main data-access operator is the first thing to check
Per-operator cost percentage shows where the expensive part of the plan actually is
A large estimated-vs-actual row count gap signals the optimizer's assumptions were wrong

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly shows how to capture the actual execution plan
Correctly explains Seek vs. Scan and cost percentage
Mentions the estimated-vs-actual row count check

questions.title: Write a basic dbatools PowerShell script for a DBA task
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell script using the dbatools module that connects to a SQL Server instance and lists every database's name, size in MB, and recovery model, sorted by size descending.
questions.code: # Goal: Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance ... | Select-Object Name, SizeMB, RecoveryModel | Sort-Object SizeMB -Descending
questions.modelAnswer: dbatools is a community PowerShell module purpose-built for SQL Server administration -- it wraps common DBA tasks (checking databases, running backups, checking jobs, migrating logins) into straightforward cmdlets, instead of a DBA having to hand-write SMO or ADO.NET calls themselves. Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance <server> returns one object per database on that instance with properties already including Name, SizeMB, and RecoveryModel, so no manual byte-math or SMO object traversal is needed. Piping that into Sort-Object SizeMB -Descending reorders the same objects by size without altering them, exactly like Sort-Object behaves on any other PowerShell object.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance 'SQL01' | Select-Object Name, SizeMB, RecoveryModel | Sort-Object SizeMB -Descending, and the thing I'd point out to someone newer to this is that dbatools is doing a lot of work for me behind that one cmdlet -- it's already connected, queried the relevant system views, and handed back clean, typed objects with SizeMB and RecoveryModel as real properties, not something I'd have to compute myself from raw system catalog views. I reach for dbatools over hand-written T-SQL wrapped in Invoke-Sqlcmd specifically because its cmdlets are purpose-built for exactly this kind of DBA inventory and automation task, and they're consistent across hundreds of similar commands, so the pattern I learn here -- Get-DbaX, pipe to Select-Object, pipe to Sort-Object -- transfers directly to checking jobs, logins, or backups later.

Import-Module dbatools

Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance 'SQL01' |
    Select-Object Name, SizeMB, RecoveryModel |

Sorting on a string-formatted size value instead of the underlying numeric SizeMB property

Get-DbaDatabase returns one object per database with properties like Name, SizeMB, RecoveryModel
Select-Object narrows displayed properties; Sort-Object orders by a real property
The Get-DbaX / Select-Object / Sort-Object pattern is consistent across most dbatools cmdlets

questions.title: Write differential and transaction log backup statements
questions.prompt: Given a database that already has a full backup, write the T-SQL for a differential backup and a transaction log backup of that same database, and explain what each one actually restores relative to that full backup.
questions.code: -- Goal: BACKUP DATABASE ... WITH DIFFERENTIAL, and BACKUP LOG ...
questions.modelAnswer: A differential backup (BACKUP DATABASE <name> TO DISK = '<path>' WITH DIFFERENTIAL) captures only the data pages that have changed since the last full backup -- not since the last differential -- so every differential in a chain is restored directly on top of the same full backup, not on top of each other. A transaction log backup (BACKUP LOG <name> TO DISK = '<path>') captures the log records written since the last log backup, and restoring it replays those transactions, which is what enables restoring to a precise point in time, not just to the moment a full or differential backup finished. A realistic restore sequence is: restore the full backup WITH NORECOVERY, then the most recent differential WITH NORECOVERY, then every log backup taken after that differential in order, with the very last one restored WITH RECOVERY to bring the database back online.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write BACKUP DATABASE SalesDB TO DISK = 'C:\Backups\SalesDB_Diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL, COMPRESSION for the differential, and BACKUP LOG SalesDB TO DISK = 'C:\Backups\SalesDB_Log.trn' WITH COMPRESSION for the log backup. The detail I'd make sure to get right in an interview is that a differential always measures its changes against the last full backup, never against the previous differential -- so I only ever need the full plus the single most recent differential to restore to that differential's point, not a whole chain of differentials. Log backups are what actually let me go further than that, restoring transaction by transaction up to a specific moment. My restore sequence would be: full WITH NORECOVERY, latest differential WITH NORECOVERY, then every log backup taken since that differential in order, with only the final one using WITH RECOVERY to bring the database back online.
commonMistakes: Assuming a differential backs up changes since the last differential, rather than always since the last full backup
Restoring differentials one after another in a chain instead of just the single most recent one on top of the full
Forgetting WITH NORECOVERY on every restore step except the very last one, which locks the database in a restoring state or ends recovery too early
Taking log backups on a database still in SIMPLE recovery model, where they aren't meaningful at all
keyPoints: A differential captures changes since the last full backup, not since the last differential
A log backup captures log records since the last log backup, enabling point-in-time restore
Restore order: full (NORECOVERY), latest differential (NORECOVERY), logs in order, last step WITH RECOVERY
Log backups require FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct BACKUP DATABASE WITH DIFFERENTIAL and BACKUP LOG syntax
Correctly explains what each backup type captures relative to the full backup
Describes a correct restore sequence with NORECOVERY/RECOVERY

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Cartesian product and the row-count math
Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
Describes a practical way to catch this before production

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: A new client IP suddenly can't connect to Azure SQL Database
questions.prompt: A developer who could connect to an Azure SQL Database from their laptop yesterday gets 'Cannot open server ... requested by the login. Client with IP address ... is not allowed to access the server' today, and nothing about their credentials or the database changed. What's going on, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Azure SQL's server-level firewall allows connections only from explicitly allowed client IP ranges; the error message is literal, not a credentials issue -- the request never reaches authentication at all because the firewall blocks it earlier. The most common cause for someone who connected fine yesterday is a changed public IP, which happens routinely on home/ISP connections without a static IP, or on a laptop that moved networks (coffee shop, VPN, office). The fix is adding a new firewall rule for the current IP (or range) on the server (or at the database level for a per-database rule), ideally scoped as narrowly as practical rather than opening a wide range permanently; Azure also offers 'Allow Azure services' as a separate toggle, which is unrelated to a specific client IP and shouldn't be used to work around this for a human developer's laptop.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd check the exact IP address named in the error message first, since Azure's firewall error is unusually literal about what it blocked. Nine times out of ten for 'it worked yesterday,' the developer's public IP changed overnight -- a home ISP connection without a static IP, or they're now on a different network than yesterday (coffee shop, VPN, a different office). The fix is adding that specific IP (or a narrow range around it) as a new server-level firewall rule, either through the portal's Networking blade or with sp_set_firewall_rule, rather than widening the rule to something careless like 0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255 just to make the problem go away permanently. I'd also make sure not to reach for the separate 'Allow Azure services' toggle here, since that's meant for Azure-hosted services connecting, not a human's laptop on a home network.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's a credentials/password problem and resetting the login instead of checking the firewall
Opening an overly broad IP range (0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255) as a lazy permanent fix
Forgetting database-level firewall rules are separate from server-level ones
Not realizing 'Allow Azure services' doesn't help a client connecting from a home or office network
keyPoints: Azure SQL firewall blocks at the network layer, before authentication
The error names the blocked client IP directly
A home/ISP IP change or a network switch is the most common cause of a sudden block
Add a scoped firewall rule for the current IP rather than a blanket allow-all

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the firewall (not credentials) as the cause
Identifies the likely IP-change scenario
Proposes a correctly scoped fix
