questions.title: Queries that were fast yesterday are suddenly slow with no code changes
questions.prompt: A DTU-based Azure SQL Database that normally responds quickly starts timing out and running slowly during business hours, even though no query or schema changed recently. What would you check first, and what's a likely root cause?
questions.modelAnswer: With a DTU model, compute, memory, and I/O are bundled into one blended resource ceiling for the tier -- once the workload's actual demand (more concurrent users, a bigger batch job, growing data volume) pushes resource consumption to that ceiling, every query on the database gets throttled, not just one bad query. The first check is Azure Monitor metrics for that database -- DTU percentage, CPU percentage, and data IO percentage -- during the slow window; sustained time near 100% on any of those is the signal. A likely root cause for 'nothing changed in the code' is that the workload itself grew (more rows, more concurrent sessions, a new reporting job someone scheduled) past what the current tier can handle, not a query regression. The fix is either tuning away unnecessary load, or scaling up to a higher DTU tier (or migrating to vCore for more granular control) rather than hunting for a single bad query that doesn't exist.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go straight to Azure Monitor and pull up the database's DTU percentage, CPU percentage, and Data IO percentage metrics for the exact window things got slow, before looking at any individual query. With DTU, those three resources are bundled into one ceiling, so once the workload's actual demand grows -- more concurrent users, a bigger overnight job someone added, the data itself just growing -- the whole database gets throttled together, not one specific query. 'Nothing in the code changed' doesn't rule that out at all; the workload growing against a fixed ceiling is just as common a cause as a query regression, and I've seen that trip people up because they go looking for a bad query that was never actually the problem. If the metrics confirm it, the fix is either reducing unnecessary load or scaling the tier up, not continuing to tune queries that were already fine.
commonMistakes: Assuming a code or query change must be the cause, when workload growth against a fixed resource ceiling is just as common
Not checking Azure Monitor's DTU/CPU/IO percentage metrics first
Trying to fix a resource-ceiling problem by only tuning indexes, when scaling up may be what's actually needed
Not realizing DTU bundles three resources together, which can hide which one is actually maxed out
keyPoints: DTU throttles the whole database once its blended resource ceiling is hit
Check Azure Monitor's DTU/CPU/IO percentage metrics first
'Nothing in the code changed' doesn't rule out workload growth as the cause
The fix may be scaling the tier, not just query tuning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies checking resource metrics first
Correctly explains the DTU blended-ceiling throttling behavior
Proposes a sensible fix (scale or reduce load)

questions.title: An application can't authenticate to Azure SQL even though SSMS connects fine
questions.prompt: A DBA can connect to an Azure SQL Database from SSMS using 'Microsoft Entra MFA' authentication with their own account, but an application's connection string, which is supposed to authenticate via a different method, fails with a login error. The DBA insists 'the database works fine, I just tested it.' What's the gap in that reasoning, and what would you check?
questions.modelAnswer: Testing a personal, interactive, MFA-based login proves the database is reachable and that the DBA's own identity has access -- it proves nothing about whether the application's identity (commonly a different Entra service principal, managed identity, or a SQL login) has been granted a user and permissions inside that specific database, or whether its authentication method is even configured correctly. The checks are: has a corresponding database user actually been created for the application's identity (CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for an Entra identity, not just a server-level login); does that user have the permissions the application's queries need; and does the application's connection string specify an authentication mode (Active Directory Integrated, Service Principal, etc.) that matches how that identity is actually set up in Entra ID. 'I tested it and it works' with a different identity and a different auth path doesn't test any of that.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that the DBA's test only proves their own identity, using their own auth method, can reach the database -- it tells us nothing about a completely different identity using a completely different authentication path. The first thing I'd check is whether a database user actually exists for the application's identity -- for an Entra identity that means CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER run inside this specific database, not just that identity existing somewhere in Entra ID generally. Then I'd check what permissions that user actually has, since existing isn't the same as being allowed to do anything. And I'd compare the authentication mode in the connection string against how that identity is really configured -- a managed identity, a service principal, and an Entra user all authenticate differently, and a mismatch there fails just as hard as a missing user would.
commonMistakes: Treating a successful personal login as proof the database works for every identity and every auth method
Forgetting an Entra identity still needs CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER inside the specific database, not just existing in Entra ID
Mismatching the authentication mode in the connection string against how the identity is actually configured
Not checking whether the application's identity has actually been granted any permissions at all
keyPoints: A successful personal/interactive login doesn't validate a different identity's access
An Entra identity needs its own database user created inside each database, not just existing in Entra ID
The connection string's authentication mode must match the identity's actual configuration
Check permissions granted to that specific identity, not just reachability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the gap in the DBA's reasoning
Correctly describes checking the database user/permissions for the app's identity
Mentions matching the connection string's auth mode to the identity's configuration

questions.title: A backup job shows as 'succeeded' but the backup file is missing
questions.prompt: A SQL Server Agent job that runs a nightly backup shows a green 'Succeeded' status in the job history every night, but when you go looking for yesterday's backup file, it isn't there. What are the first things you'd check?
questions.modelAnswer: A job step reporting success only means the T-SQL or command it ran returned without an error -- it doesn't guarantee the step's logic actually did what was intended. Common causes: the job step's backup path points somewhere other than where you're looking (a typo, or a path that changed after a server move, pointing to a now-unused or unreachable location that happened not to error); a separate cleanup/maintenance job is deleting old backup files on a schedule that's quietly also deleting this one; or the job is actually succeeding against a different database/server than expected (an environment mismatch in the step's connection or variables). The checks, in order: open the job step and confirm the exact backup path and database name it's actually running against; check the step's own output log, not just the overall job history's green status, since a step can 'succeed' per SQL Agent while still doing something unintended; check whether a retention/cleanup job runs after the backup job and could be removing the file.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop trusting the green 'Succeeded' status as proof of anything beyond 'the command didn't error,' and go open the actual job step to see exactly what path and database it's configured against -- a typo in the path, or a path that was valid before a server move and quietly isn't anymore, is a surprisingly common cause, and it won't necessarily throw an error if the step still technically completes. Next I'd pull the step's detailed output log rather than just the job history's overall status, since the output often shows the real path it wrote to, which might not match where I've been looking. And I'd specifically check whether there's a separate cleanup or retention job scheduled to run after this one, since I've seen a well-intentioned 'delete backups older than 7 days' job accidentally catch files it shouldn't have.
commonMistakes: Trusting the green 'Succeeded' status as proof the backup file physically exists where expected
Not checking the step's own detailed output/log, only the job history's overall status
Overlooking a separate cleanup job that might be deleting files on its own schedule
Not verifying the job is pointed at the intended database and path at all
keyPoints: Job success means the step ran without error, not that its outcome matches intent
Check the step's actual configured path/database, not just the job name
Review the step's detailed output log, not just the overall history status
Check for a separate retention/cleanup job that could be removing the file afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that 'Succeeded' doesn't guarantee the intended outcome
Describes a logical, specific set of checks
Considers a separate cleanup job as a possible cause

questions.title: Diagnosing a blocked session with DMVs
questions.prompt: Several users report a report they run daily has been hanging for several minutes instead of returning instantly like usual. How would you use DMVs to find out whether a session is actually blocked, and by what?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is querying sys.dm_exec_requests and looking at the blocking_session_id column for the hanging session's session_id -- a non-zero value there means this session is actively waiting on a lock held by that other session_id, which is the head/root cause worth investigating, not the symptom itself. Once the blocking session is identified, checking what that blocking session is actually doing (its last_request_start_time, its own wait_type, and whether it's idle with an open transaction versus actively running something) usually explains the chain -- a very common beginner-level case is someone running a query in SSMS, getting the result, but never committing or rolling back an open transaction, leaving locks held indefinitely while they've walked away from their desk. sys.dm_tran_locks can be joined in for more detail on exactly which resource (which table, which row or page) is being contested, though for a beginner-level diagnosis, just identifying the blocking_session_id and what it's doing is usually enough to know who to go talk to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run a query against sys.dm_exec_requests and look specifically at blocking_session_id for the session that's hanging -- if that column is anything other than 0, I've found my answer: this session isn't slow, it's stuck waiting on a lock held by whatever session_id shows up there. From there I'd look at that blocking session specifically -- what's its last_request_start_time, is it actively running something or just sitting idle. The classic beginner-level case I've run into more than once is a developer who ran an UPDATE in SSMS, got their result, and then got pulled into a meeting without ever hitting commit or rollback -- that session is sitting there idle, but it's still holding every lock from that open transaction, and everyone else waiting on those same rows just queues up behind it. Once I see that pattern, the fix is usually just getting that person to commit or roll back, not tuning any query at all.
questions.example:
-- Is anything actively blocked right now, and by whom?
SELECT session_id, status, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, last_request_start_time
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- What is the blocking session itself doing?
SELECT session_id, status, last_request_start_time, open_transaction_count
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = <blocking_session_id>;
commonMistakes: Assuming a hanging query must be poorly written, without checking blocking_session_id first
Not realizing an idle session can still hold locks indefinitely if it has an open, uncommitted transaction
Killing the blocked session instead of investigating and addressing the session that's actually causing the block
Not checking the blocking session's own status, missing that it's sitting idle rather than running something legitimate
keyPoints: sys.dm_exec_requests.blocking_session_id identifies whether, and by whom, a session is blocked
A session can be idle yet still block others if it holds an open, uncommitted transaction
Investigate and address the blocking session, not just the symptom (the blocked one)
sys.dm_tran_locks adds detail on exactly which resource is contested, if needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses blocking_session_id to identify the blocker
Correctly explains how an idle session can still hold locks
Focuses the fix on the blocking session, not the symptom

questions.title: A migrated Oracle batch job silently loses changes
questions.prompt: A SQL Server DBA writes a quick script against a newly stood-up Oracle database, the same way they always would in SQL Server: run a few INSERT statements in SQL*Plus, see 'rows created' messages, and move on without explicitly ending the session with anything. The next day, none of those rows are actually there. What assumption from SQL Server broke, and what should they have done differently?
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server, by default, runs in autocommit mode -- each individual statement is its own transaction and is committed automatically the instant it succeeds, unless the DBA explicitly starts a BEGIN TRANSACTION. Oracle's default behavior is the opposite: statements run inside an implicit transaction that stays open until an explicit COMMIT (or ROLLBACK) is issued, and a session ending without one -- a disconnect, a crash, or simply exiting the tool -- rolls that open transaction back automatically rather than committing it. The DBA's mistake was carrying over the SQL Server assumption that a successful-looking statement is already durable; in Oracle, 'rows created' only means the statement executed without error inside the still-open transaction, not that the data is actually saved. The fix is forming the habit of issuing an explicit COMMIT after the work is verified correct (and knowing ROLLBACK is available if it isn't), rather than assuming the session ending cleanly is equivalent to committing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name the exact assumption that broke: in SQL Server, I'm used to a statement being committed the moment it succeeds, since autocommit is the default and I only get a multi-statement transaction if I deliberately write BEGIN TRANSACTION. Oracle flips that -- by default, work sits inside an open transaction until I explicitly type COMMIT, and if that session just ends without one, Oracle rolls it back rather than keeping it, which is exactly what happened here. 'Rows created' from SQL*Plus is Oracle telling me the statement itself succeeded, not that the data survived past the session -- those are two different facts I'm used to treating as the same thing in SQL Server. Going forward, the habit I'd build immediately when working in Oracle is typing COMMIT (or deliberately ROLLBACK if something looks wrong) as a conscious, separate step every single time, rather than trusting that finishing a script cleanly is the same as the data being saved.
commonMistakes: Assuming Oracle autocommits by default the same way SQL Server does
Treating a successful-looking statement message ('rows created') as proof the data is already durable
Not knowing a disconnected or ended Oracle session rolls back an uncommitted transaction automatically
Never forming the explicit COMMIT/ROLLBACK habit when moving from a platform where autocommit is the default
keyPoints: SQL Server defaults to autocommit per statement; Oracle defaults to an open transaction until an explicit COMMIT
A successful statement message isn't proof the work is durable in Oracle
An Oracle session ending without a COMMIT rolls back its open transaction automatically
Build the explicit COMMIT/ROLLBACK habit deliberately when working in Oracle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the autocommit-vs-explicit-commit difference
Correctly explains why the rows disappeared (rollback on disconnect)
Proposes the correct habit/fix going forward

lessonLink.label: Review: Relational Concepts That Transfer vs. What Doesn't

questions.title: A MongoDB collection modeled exactly like relational tables performs badly
questions.prompt: A developer new to MongoDB, coming from a SQL Server background, models a blog application with separate 'Posts' and 'Comments' collections, linking comments back to posts by a PostID field, and writing a separate query to fetch a post's comments every time a post is displayed -- effectively treating MongoDB like it has joins. Performance is noticeably worse than they expected. What's the modeling mismatch, and how would you advise fixing it?
questions.modelAnswer: The mismatch is bringing a relational, always-normalize mental model into MongoDB, which doesn't have a native, efficient join the way SQL Server does -- MongoDB does support a $lookup aggregation stage that can approximate a join, but it's generally less efficient than embedding, and reaching for it as the default pattern defeats much of the reason to use a document database in the first place. Because comments are read together with their post almost every time a post is displayed, and the relationship is naturally one-to-many with a bounded, reasonable number of comments per post, this is a textbook case for embedding: storing each post's comments as a nested array directly inside that post's own document, so retrieving a post and all of its comments is a single document read instead of two separate queries (or a $lookup) stitched together in application code. The general modeling guidance that should replace the relational instinct here is to design around how the data is actually read together, not around normalizing every relationship into its own separate collection by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name what's happening: the developer is still thinking in SQL Server terms -- normalize everything into separate tables, join when you need the combined view -- and MongoDB doesn't reward that pattern the same way, because it doesn't have an efficient native join. It does have $lookup, but reaching for it as a MongoDB-flavored replacement for every SQL Server join usually means missing the actual point of a document database. Since a post's comments are almost always read together with the post itself, and there's a reasonable, bounded number of comments per post, I'd advise embedding the comments as an array directly inside the post document. Reading a post then becomes one single document fetch instead of a query plus a join (or a second round trip), which is both simpler code and genuinely faster. The mental shift I'd want them to make permanently is designing the document around 'what gets read together,' not around 'how would I normalize this in SQL Server,' since those two questions often point to different structures.
commonMistakes: Carrying over the relational instinct to always normalize into separate collections by default
Treating $lookup as a drop-in replacement for a SQL JOIN rather than recognizing embedding is usually the better fit here
Not considering how the data is actually read together when deciding the document structure
Assuming MongoDB performance problems are solved the same way SQL Server ones are (an index), without first questioning the schema design itself
keyPoints: MongoDB has no efficient native join; $lookup exists but isn't a drop-in replacement for relational joins
Embedding related, together-read data (like comments in a post) avoids extra queries/joins entirely
Design the document structure around how data is actually read together, not around relational normalization habits
A bounded one-to-many relationship read together is a textbook case for embedding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the relational-modeling mismatch as the root cause
Correctly recommends embedding over a $lookup-based join pattern
Articulates the general 'design around how data is read' principle

lessonLink.label: Review: Embedding vs. Referencing: Schema Design Patterns

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

lessonLink.label: Review: SDLC: Dev, QA, UAT & Production

questions.title: Choosing between Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and a VM
questions.prompt: A company is migrating an on-prem SQL Server that uses SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and linked servers extensively. Which of Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, or SQL Server on an Azure VM is the best starting fit, and why would the other two be a worse fit for this specific workload?
questions.modelAnswer: Azure SQL Database is a single-database PaaS service -- it doesn't support cross-database queries or linked servers in the way on-prem SQL Server does, and SQL Server Agent doesn't exist there at all (Elastic Jobs is a different, more limited substitute), so a workload actively depending on those features would need significant re-architecture to move there. Azure SQL Managed Instance is purpose-built for close instance-level compatibility: it supports SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries within the instance, and linked servers, while still being a managed PaaS service with automated patching and backups -- making it the best fit here, since it minimizes the re-architecture work this specific workload would otherwise require. SQL Server on an Azure VM (IaaS) would also technically support all of these features since it's just SQL Server, but it would be a worse fit than Managed Instance specifically because the customer is back to patching the OS and SQL Server themselves, managing their own backups and HA, rather than getting that managed automatically -- VM is the right call only when a workload needs something even Managed Instance can't do (a specific unsupported feature or version).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as lifting the instance's actual behavior, not just its data. Azure SQL Database would force a real re-architecture here, since it doesn't have SQL Server Agent at all, and it can't do cross-database queries or linked servers the way this workload depends on. SQL Server on a VM would technically support everything this workload does today, since it's genuinely SQL Server, but it hands all the OS patching, SQL Server patching, and backup/HA management back to the team, which is exactly the operational burden a cloud migration is usually trying to reduce. Managed Instance sits right in the middle on purpose -- it keeps SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, and linked servers working close to how they do today, while still being a managed PaaS service, which is why I'd start there and only drop down to a VM if something turns up that even Managed Instance genuinely can't support.
commonMistakes: Picking Azure SQL Database by default without checking for instance-level features like SQL Server Agent or cross-database queries that it doesn't support
Assuming VM is always 'safest' since it's most like on-prem, ignoring the operational burden it brings back
Not recognizing Managed Instance exists specifically to bridge this gap
Assuming all three options cost the same operational effort
keyPoints: Azure SQL Database doesn't support cross-database queries, linked servers, or SQL Server Agent
Managed Instance supports those while remaining a managed PaaS service
VM supports everything SQL Server does but returns OS/patching/backup responsibility to the customer
Match the service to the workload's actual instance-level dependencies, not just 'it's a SQL Server workload'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies Managed Instance as the best fit
Correctly explains why Azure SQL Database is a poor fit here
Correctly explains the operational tradeoff of choosing a VM instead

questions.title: High availability and disaster recovery are not the same thing
questions.prompt: A manager says 'we have Always On Availability Groups configured, so we're covered for disasters.' What's the gap in that statement, and how would you explain the difference between high availability and disaster recovery to them?
questions.modelAnswer: High availability protects against a failure within a site -- a server, a disk, a single piece of hardware going down -- by automatically failing over to another node that's already running, typically within the same datacenter or nearby, aiming for minutes of disruption or less. Disaster recovery protects against losing an entire site -- a datacenter outage, a regional disaster -- and depends on having a copy of the data and a way to run the workload somewhere genuinely separate, which usually takes longer to fail over to and may lose a small amount of the most recent data depending on the replication method. An Availability Group configured entirely within one datacenter (or even across AZs in a single region) is an HA solution -- it does nothing if that entire region becomes unavailable. True DR requires a replica (or geo-replication, or a failover group) that lives in a genuinely separate region, with its own tested failover plan and a defined RPO/RTO.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the gap with a concrete scenario: an Availability Group with all its replicas in the same region protects us beautifully if one server dies -- we fail over in seconds and barely notice. It does absolutely nothing if that entire region goes down, because every single replica we have is sitting in the same place. That's the actual difference: HA covers a local hardware failure with a fast failover to a nearby node; DR covers losing an entire site, which needs a genuinely separate region, its own tested plan, and its own RPO/RTO targets that are usually looser than HA's, since failing over across regions takes longer and can lose slightly more recent data. I'd tell the manager we're covered for one kind of disaster and not the other, and ask what our actual tolerance is for losing a whole region before we decide whether that gap needs closing.
commonMistakes: Treating same-datacenter or same-region redundancy as disaster coverage
Assuming any kind of 'redundancy' automatically means DR is solved
Not having a tested, specific plan and RPO/RTO target for the actual disaster scenario
Conflating a failover test for HA with a failover test for DR, which are different drills
keyPoints: HA = protects against a local hardware/node failure, fast failover, same site
DR = protects against losing an entire site/region, requires genuinely separate location and a tested plan
Same-region or same-datacenter redundancy alone is not DR
HA and DR need separate, explicit RPO/RTO targets

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes HA from DR
Correctly identifies the gap in the manager's statement
Mentions the need for a genuinely separate region and tested plan for real DR

questions.title: Translating a business requirement into RPO and RTO
questions.prompt: A stakeholder says 'if we ever lose the database, we can't afford to lose more than 15 minutes of data, and we need to be back up within an hour.' Translate that into the two specific technical terms a DBA would actually design around, and explain what each one constrains.
questions.modelAnswer: 'Can't lose more than 15 minutes of data' is the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) -- the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time, which directly constrains how frequently (or how continuously) data must be backed up or replicated; a 15-minute RPO rules out a backup strategy that only takes transaction log backups every hour, for example. 'Back up within an hour' is the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) -- the maximum acceptable length of the outage itself, which constrains the failover/restore mechanism chosen, since restoring a large database from a cold backup might take far longer than an hour, pushing the design toward a warm standby or automated failover instead. The two are independent and both need an explicit design response -- a tight RTO with a loose RPO (or vice versa) calls for a genuinely different architecture than tight-tight or loose-loose.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd translate it directly: '15 minutes of data loss' is the RPO, and it tells me how often I need to be backing up or replicating -- hourly log backups wouldn't cut it, I'd need something closer to continuous or every 15 minutes at most. 'Back up within an hour' is the RTO, and it's really asking about the failover mechanism, not the backup frequency -- if restoring from a cold backup realistically takes three hours on a database this size, an hour-long RTO means I need a warm standby or an automated failover path, not a restore-from-backup plan. The thing I'd make sure the stakeholder understands is that these are two separate numbers driving two separate parts of the design, and giving me both up front is exactly what lets me design the right thing instead of guessing.
commonMistakes: Confusing RPO (data loss tolerance) with RTO (downtime tolerance) -- they constrain different things
Assuming a single backup/replication strategy automatically satisfies both without checking the actual numbers
Not realizing a tight RTO usually requires a warm standby/automated failover rather than restoring from backup
Treating these as soft goals rather than specific numbers the architecture must be designed to meet
keyPoints: RPO = maximum acceptable data loss, constrains backup/replication frequency
RTO = maximum acceptable downtime, constrains the failover/restore mechanism
The two are independent and both need explicit numbers
A tight RTO typically requires a warm standby, not just backups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly translates the requirement into RPO and RTO
Correctly explains what each term constrains
Recognizes the two require independent design decisions

questions.title: Choosing public endpoint, VNet service endpoint, or private endpoint
questions.prompt: At a beginner level, what are the three basic options for how an application connects to Azure SQL Database over the network, and what's the one-sentence reason to pick a private endpoint over the public endpoint with firewall rules?
questions.modelAnswer: The public endpoint with firewall rules reaches the database over the public internet, restricted to allowed IP addresses -- simple to set up, but the database still has a public-facing address at all, which some security policies disallow outright. A VNet service endpoint restricts access to traffic coming from a specific virtual network, still over Microsoft's backbone rather than the open internet, without giving the database its own private IP address inside that VNet. A private endpoint goes further, giving the database an actual private IP address inside the VNet, so traffic never touches a public endpoint at all -- the one-sentence reason to choose it over the public endpoint is that a private endpoint removes the database's public internet exposure entirely, which both public-endpoint-with-firewall and VNet-service-endpoint still retain in some form.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay out the three options from least to most restrictive. Public endpoint with firewall rules is the simplest -- the database is reachable over the internet, but only from IP addresses I've explicitly allowed. A VNet service endpoint tightens that further, restricting traffic to a specific virtual network over Microsoft's own backbone, though the database still doesn't get a real private IP of its own. A private endpoint is the strongest option -- the database actually gets a private IP address inside my VNet, so there's no public-facing address to reach at all. If someone asks why go all the way to a private endpoint instead of just firewall rules, my one-sentence answer is that it removes the database's public internet exposure entirely, which firewall rules alone never actually do -- they just restrict who can reach that still-public address.
commonMistakes: Assuming firewall rules alone remove public exposure, when the public endpoint is still technically internet-facing
Confusing a VNet service endpoint (restricts by source network, no private IP) with a private endpoint (gives the resource an actual private IP)
Picking the most restrictive option by default without checking the application's actual connectivity needs
Not knowing a private endpoint can coexist with disabling the public endpoint entirely
keyPoints: Public endpoint + firewall = internet-facing, IP-restricted
VNet service endpoint = traffic restricted to a VNet, still no private IP on the database
Private endpoint = database gets a real private IP inside the VNet, no public exposure
Private endpoint is the strongest option for removing internet exposure entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all three connectivity options
Correctly states the one-sentence reason to prefer a private endpoint

questions.title: Point-in-time restore vs. long-term retention
questions.prompt: Azure SQL Database automatically keeps backups for point-in-time restore. Why isn't that enough to satisfy a compliance requirement to keep a yearly backup for 7 years, and what feature actually covers that?
questions.modelAnswer: Automated point-in-time restore (PITR) backups exist specifically to recover from a recent mistake or outage -- their retention window is short (commonly 7-35 days depending on tier) because that's the realistic window for 'restore to right before someone ran a bad UPDATE,' not a compliance archive. A 7-year yearly retention requirement is a completely different use case -- long-term retention (LTR) -- which is a separate, explicitly configured policy that takes weekly full backups and retains them on a much longer schedule (up to 10 years) specifically to satisfy requirements like this. The two are not redundant: PITR protects operational recovery over days/weeks; LTR must be deliberately configured if any backup needs to survive past that short window.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that the automatic point-in-time restore window is deliberately short -- it's designed for 'someone ran a bad UPDATE an hour ago, let's roll back to right before it,' not for a seven-year compliance archive, so by the time a year has passed, that backup is long gone under the default policy. The feature that actually covers a seven-year requirement is long-term retention, which is a completely separate, explicitly configured policy -- it isn't on by default, and it has to be set up to take and retain weekly full backups on whatever schedule the compliance requirement actually calls for, up to 10 years. I'd make sure to configure LTR specifically once I know the exact retention number required, rather than assuming the default PITR window has it covered.
commonMistakes: Assuming the default PITR window covers any retention requirement, including multi-year ones
Not realizing LTR must be explicitly configured -- it isn't on by default
Confusing PITR's purpose (operational recovery) with LTR's purpose (compliance/archival)
Not checking the actual regulatory requirement's specific retention length before configuring LTR
keyPoints: PITR = short automatic retention window for operational recovery (days to weeks)
LTR = separate, explicitly configured long-term policy (up to 10 years) for compliance
The two serve different purposes and aren't interchangeable
LTR is not on by default and must be deliberately set up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why PITR alone doesn't satisfy the requirement
Correctly identifies LTR as the feature that covers it
Notes LTR must be explicitly configured

questions.title: Designing database access with least privilege
questions.prompt: A new reporting application only needs to read data from a handful of tables. A developer asks you to just add its service account to the db_owner role 'to keep things simple.' How would you push back, and what would you actually grant instead?
questions.modelAnswer: db_owner grants full control over the database -- the ability to alter schema, drop tables, modify any data, and manage permissions -- which is wildly beyond what a read-only reporting application needs, and turns any bug, credential leak, or compromised connection string in that application into a full-database incident instead of a contained one. The principle of least privilege says to grant only the specific permissions actually required for the task -- here, SELECT on the specific tables or views the report reads from, ideally through a dedicated database role created for that purpose (CREATE ROLE ReportingReader; GRANT SELECT ON ... TO ReportingReader; then adding the service account's user to that role) rather than granting broad permissions directly to the account. This also makes future auditing straightforward -- the role's name and its grants describe exactly what it's for.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back by naming the actual risk, not just the principle: if that reporting app's connection string ever leaks, or there's a bug in how it builds a query, db_owner means whoever or whatever exploits that can drop tables or rewrite data, not just read a report wrong. What I'd grant instead is a purpose-built role -- create a ReportingReader role, grant it SELECT on just the specific tables or views the report actually touches, and add the service account to that role rather than granting anything directly to the account itself. That also pays off later: six months from now, anyone auditing access can see exactly what ReportingReader is for just from its name and its grants, instead of having to reverse-engineer why a reporting account somehow has db_owner.
commonMistakes: Granting db_owner (or sysadmin) 'to keep things simple' or to avoid a permissions-debugging conversation
Granting permissions directly to an individual account instead of through a named role
Not revisiting broad grants later once the 'temporary' simplification becomes permanent
Not scoping SELECT to only the specific tables/views actually needed
keyPoints: db_owner grants full control, far beyond what a read-only app needs
Least privilege means granting only the specific permissions the task requires
Use a named database role rather than granting directly to an account
A narrowly-scoped role is easier to audit and reason about later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why db_owner is excessive for this use case
Proposes a correctly-scoped role-based grant
Mentions the auditing benefit of a purpose-named role

questions.title: Deciding between IaaS and PaaS for a new SQL Server workload
questions.prompt: A team needs a new SQL Server database for an internal application and isn't sure whether to provision a SQL Server VM (IaaS) or Azure SQL Database (PaaS). What questions would you ask to help them decide, and what's the core tradeoff?
questions.modelAnswer: The core tradeoff is control versus operational burden. PaaS (Azure SQL Database/Managed Instance) hands patching, OS management, automated backups, and built-in HA to Microsoft, in exchange for giving up some control -- no OS-level access, no installing arbitrary software alongside SQL Server, and some SQL Server features/versions are unavailable. IaaS (SQL Server on a VM) gives full control over the OS and SQL Server configuration, including anything that depends on OS-level access or an unsupported SQL Server feature/version, but the customer is back to patching, backup strategy, and HA/DR design themselves. The questions that actually settle it: does this workload need OS-level access, a specific unsupported SQL feature, or a legacy SQL Server version? Is there a team with the time and expertise to keep patching and backups running correctly long-term, or would that realistically get neglected? If nothing requires OS-level control, PaaS is almost always the better default for a new internal application.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with one question: does anything about this workload actually require OS-level access, a specific unsupported SQL Server feature, or a legacy version that PaaS doesn't offer? If the honest answer is no, PaaS is almost always the right default, because Microsoft takes patching, backups, and HA infrastructure off the team's plate entirely, and that's real, ongoing work being avoided, not just a one-time setup convenience. The second question I'd ask is more about the team than the technology: is there realistically someone who's going to keep patching this VM and verifying backups actually work, six months from now, when it's no longer a new and exciting project? I've seen 'we'll handle it ourselves' VMs quietly fall behind on patches because nobody owned that ongoing responsibility. The core tradeoff really is control versus operational burden -- IaaS gives full control at the cost of owning all of that upkeep; PaaS gives up some control in exchange for Microsoft owning it instead.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a VM because it feels 'safer' or more familiar, without checking whether anything actually requires OS-level access
Not accounting for the ongoing operational cost of patching/backups when choosing IaaS
Assuming PaaS can't be migrated to later if requirements genuinely change, when it's a real but doable migration path
Treating this as a one-time technical decision instead of asking who will realistically maintain it
keyPoints: Core tradeoff is control (IaaS) vs. operational burden handed to Microsoft (PaaS)
PaaS is the better default unless something specific requires OS-level access or an unsupported feature/version
Ask about the team's realistic ability to maintain patching/backups/HA before choosing IaaS
The decision isn't permanent, but changing later still requires real migration effort

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the core control-vs-burden tradeoff
Asks sensible, concrete decision questions
Gives a reasonable default recommendation

questions.title: Why on-prem SQL Server needs an explicit backup strategy design
questions.prompt: A junior DBA, used to hearing that 'the cloud handles backups automatically,' asks why an on-prem SQL Server environment needs someone to deliberately design a full/differential/log backup cadence at all, instead of just turning a setting on. How would you explain the architectural difference?
questions.modelAnswer: Azure SQL Database automates backup scheduling and retention as a built-in platform feature, because Microsoft owns and operates the underlying infrastructure and can bake a default backup cadence into the service itself. On-prem SQL Server has no such platform wrapped around it -- the instance itself has no opinion about how often to back up, where to put the files, or how long to keep them; all of that is a deliberate design decision the DBA has to make and implement, typically via SQL Server Agent jobs calling BACKUP DATABASE/BACKUP LOG on a schedule. That design has to balance several real constraints that a cloud default already has pre-baked for a typical workload: how much data loss is tolerable (which sets the log backup frequency), how long a restore is allowed to take (which affects how often full/differential backups run, since a longer gap since the last full means replaying more log backups during a restore), and available storage and network bandwidth for where backups are written and how long they're retained. In short: on-prem shifts the responsibility for a decision cloud PaaS already made by default onto the DBA, and getting it wrong is discovered exactly when it matters most -- during a real restore.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that 'the cloud handles it automatically' is true specifically because Microsoft owns the whole stack underneath Azure SQL Database and has baked a sensible default cadence into the platform itself. On-prem, there's no platform making that decision for us -- SQL Server itself has zero built-in opinion about backup frequency; it just executes whatever BACKUP DATABASE or BACKUP LOG command I actually schedule through SQL Server Agent, on whatever cadence I decide. Designing that cadence means balancing real numbers: how much data we can afford to lose sets how often log backups run, how long a restore is allowed to take affects how often I take full and differential backups (since more log backups to replay means a longer restore), and I have to think through where those files physically live and how long I keep them around, none of which exists for me to configure in Azure SQL Database because it's already decided. The risk of getting this wrong on-prem is that nobody notices until the day there's an actual outage and the restore takes six hours instead of the expected one, which is a bad day to discover the gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming SQL Server itself has some built-in default backup behavior the way Azure SQL Database does
Not connecting the backup cadence design to concrete RPO/RTO numbers
Treating backup design as a one-time setup task rather than something that needs revisiting as data volume and tolerance for loss change
Not considering storage/retention and restore-time implications when designing the full/diff/log cadence
keyPoints: Azure SQL Database bakes a default backup cadence into the managed platform; on-prem SQL Server has no such default
On-prem, the DBA must deliberately design and schedule the full/diff/log cadence via Agent jobs
The cadence should be driven by concrete RPO/RTO numbers, storage, and restore-time tradeoffs
Gaps in on-prem backup design are typically discovered during a real restore, at the worst time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why on-prem has no built-in backup default, unlike PaaS
Correctly connects the cadence design to RPO/RTO and restore-time tradeoffs
Clarity of explanation for a junior audience

questions.title: When a document database fits better than a relational one
questions.prompt: At a beginner level, what kind of application workload genuinely fits a document database like MongoDB better than a relational database like SQL Server, and what should make a DBA cautious about reaching for one anyway?
questions.modelAnswer: A document database tends to fit well when an application's data naturally comes in self-contained, variably-shaped records that are mostly read and written as a whole unit -- a product catalog where different product categories have genuinely different attributes, a content-management system storing varied page layouts, or an application whose schema is still evolving quickly and would otherwise require frequent ALTER TABLE migrations in a relational design. It also fits workloads that need to scale horizontally across many servers more easily than a single relational instance typically does. The caution a DBA should bring is that flexible schema isn't free -- without the data integrity guarantees a relational database enforces by default (foreign keys, strict column types, join-based consistency checks), a document database pushes more of that correctness responsibility onto the application's own code, and a workload that's genuinely relational at its core -- lots of ad-hoc querying across many different relationships, strong consistency requirements, complex multi-table transactions -- usually still fits a relational engine better, even if the data could technically be jammed into documents.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point to workloads where the data is naturally self-contained and variably shaped -- a product catalog where electronics and clothing have completely different attributes, or a CMS storing all sorts of differently-structured page content -- as the clearest fit, since forcing that into a rigid relational schema usually means either a sparse table full of mostly-NULL columns or a constant stream of ALTER TABLE migrations as new variations show up. It also fits a team that genuinely needs to scale out across many servers more easily than a single relational instance usually allows. What I'd stay cautious about is that MongoDB's flexible schema doesn't come with the same built-in guarantees I get for free in SQL Server -- no automatic foreign-key enforcement, no strict column typing by default -- so correctness becomes more of an application-level discipline than a database-level guarantee. And if the real workload is doing a lot of ad-hoc, varied querying across many different relationships with strong consistency needs, that's usually still a better fit for a relational engine, even if someone's enthusiastic about trying something new.
commonMistakes: Choosing a document database purely because it's newer or trendier, without checking whether the data is actually variably-shaped and self-contained
Assuming schema flexibility is free, without recognizing the integrity-guarantee tradeoff that comes with it
Missing that a genuinely relational workload (heavy ad-hoc joins, strong consistency needs) usually still fits a relational engine better
Not considering horizontal scaling needs as a legitimate, concrete reason to consider a document database
keyPoints: Document databases fit self-contained, variably-shaped records that are read/written as a whole unit
They also fit workloads needing easier horizontal scale-out than a single relational instance
Flexible schema trades away built-in relational integrity guarantees (FKs, strict typing, join-based consistency)
A workload with heavy ad-hoc joins and strong consistency needs still usually fits a relational engine better

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies workloads that genuinely fit a document database
Correctly explains the integrity-guarantee tradeoff being given up
Recognizes when a relational engine is still the better fit

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.
commonMistakes: Treating stand-up like a status report to a manager instead of the team syncing with itself
Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward
keyPoints: Daily Scrum/stand-up is short, time-boxed, and team-to-team, not a report to a manager
Typical shape: what I did, what I'm doing next, what's blocking me
Name specific work, not vague progress statements
Surface blockers immediately; save detailed discussion for after stand-up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a stand-up is and its purpose
Gives a specific, well-structured example of what to say
Avoids the common vague-status-report trap

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.
commonMistakes: Quietly grinding on a ticket without flagging it, assuming asking for help makes you look unprepared
Mislabeling 'off track' (just taking longer) as 'blocked' when there's still personal progress possible
Waiting until the next stand-up to mention a blocker instead of flagging it the moment it's identified
Flagging a blocker vaguely instead of saying specifically what's needed to unblock it
keyPoints: Off Track: work is simply taking longer than planned, more time/closer look resolves it
Blocked: a hard stop entirely outside your control -- no amount of personal effort moves it forward
The test: is there anything I can still do myself right now? If no, you're blocked
Flag a blocker immediately and specifically, not quietly or vaguely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Off Track from Blocked
Gives a usable decision test for telling them apart
Describes a clear, prompt way to communicate a real blocker

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.
commonMistakes: Explaining Agile/Waterfall in the abstract without connecting it to why it benefits this stakeholder specifically
Implying sprints mean nothing gets fully finished, instead of explaining a sprint still produces a real, shippable increment
Being dismissive of the stakeholder's preference instead of explaining the real trade-off
Using unexplained jargon (backlog, increment, retrospective) instead of plain language
keyPoints: Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements but surfaces mistakes late and expensively
Agile's short cycles let the stakeholder react to real progress every 1-2 weeks, catching misunderstandings early
Connect the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest, not an abstract process lecture
Each sprint still produces a real, working increment, not an unfinished fragment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains the Agile vs. Waterfall trade-off
Connects the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the fix is confirmed instead of acknowledging the report and giving a timeframe while still investigating
Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the scheduled refresh even run)
Investigating only inside the report itself without checking whether the issue actually originates further upstream in the data pipeline
Not giving the manager a concrete time to expect an update, leaving them to wonder if it's been forgotten
keyPoints: Communicate an acknowledgment and a timeframe immediately, don't wait for the fix to say anything
Investigate by narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source (refresh status, pipeline, source data)
Check the simplest explanation first (did the scheduled load actually run) before assuming something complex
Follow up with a clear explanation once the cause is found, not just a silent fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical investigation approach, working from symptom back to source
Correctly emphasizes communicating early, before the cause is known
Clarity and professionalism of the communication described

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A sales director emails you: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's assigned territory.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a region has zero sales for the month. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the sales director directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects yesterday's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's own territory.' The thing I'd specifically flag before writing a single line of DAX is that the email never says what should happen if a region had zero sales that month -- show it as zero, blank, or leave it off the list entirely? I'd either ask the sales director directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong during UAT.
commonMistakes: Starting to build directly from the vague email instead of writing a structured user story first
Writing a user story with no acceptance criteria, leaving 'done' undefined
Silently guessing at an ambiguous detail (like the zero-sales case) instead of asking or explicitly documenting the judgment call
Writing acceptance criteria that aren't actually checkable ('looks good') instead of specific and testable
keyPoints: User story shape: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria must be specific and checkable, not vague
Explicitly surface and resolve ambiguous details (like the zero-sales edge case) before building
A story isn't ready to build until its acceptance criteria are defined

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly-shaped user story
Writes specific, checkable acceptance criteria
Identifies and resolves an ambiguous detail from the original request

questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior developer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in my capstone, I couldn't get an OLE DB Destination's fast-load mode to actually speed anything up, and I'd already tried switching the data access mode and rereading the component's tooltips with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced developer a specific question -- 'I switched to fast load, but it's still inserting one row at a time based on the execution time, here's what I've already tried' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out I still had the destination's table lock option unchecked, which was serializing the insert behind other activity on the table. Result: once I checked that option, the load time dropped noticeably, and I started checking that same setting by default on every OLE DB Destination I've built since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a reasonable attempt was made before asking for help
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result, including what was learned or applied afterward

questions.title: Why move from Data Analyst toward BI Engineering
questions.prompt: You've been working as a Data Analyst. What's actually motivating you to grow into a BI Engineer role, and what have you been doing to build toward that?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is specific about what actually changes between the two roles, not just a vague sense that BI Engineer 'sounds like a step up.' A Data Analyst typically works with data and models that already exist, answering business questions and building reports against them; a BI Engineer takes more ownership further upstream -- designing the data model itself, building and maintaining the pipelines and transformations that feed it, and being responsible for a report's reliability and performance, not just its content. A credible motivation names a specific experience that revealed that gap -- for example, repeatedly hitting the limits of what could be fixed inside a single report because the underlying model or data pipeline itself needed to change, and wanting to be the person who can make that change rather than only ever filing a request for someone else to make it. The second half of the answer should show concrete action already taken, not just intention -- specific skills being built (SQL beyond basic querying, data modeling, understanding how data gets from source systems into the model in the first place) rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific rather than giving the generic 'I want to grow' answer. What actually pushed me toward this was hitting a point, a few times, where a report had a real problem -- slow, or a number that was technically right but the model structure made it clunky to get at -- and the fix wasn't something I could make inside the report itself; it needed a change to the underlying data model or the way data was being loaded in the first place. I kept having to file that as a request for someone else and wait, and I realized I wanted to be the person who could actually make that fix. So I've been deliberately building the skills that sit upstream of where I was working before -- going deeper into SQL past basic querying, actually learning data modeling, understanding what it takes to build and maintain the pipeline that gets data into the model in the first place -- rather than just saying I want the title.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer about wanting to 'grow' without naming the actual difference between the two roles
Describing BI Engineering as just 'more advanced reporting' instead of upstream ownership (modeling, pipelines, reliability)
Stating interest without describing any concrete action already taken toward it
Not having a specific, real experience that motivated the shift
keyPoints: Names the real distinction: Analyst works within an existing model; BI Engineer owns the model/pipeline upstream of it
Motivation should come from a specific, real experience, not a vague sense of career progression
Shows concrete action already taken (specific skills being built), not just stated intention
Avoids treating BI Engineering as simply 'more advanced reporting'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two roles
Gives a specific, credible motivation
Describes concrete action already taken

questions.title: Responding to a pull request sent back for changes
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a teammate reviewed your work -- a query, a package, or a report -- and sent it back with specific changes requested. How did you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing professionalism and how a candidate handles feedback, not a request for a technical fact. A strong answer first frames code/report review correctly: it happens inside the Dev stage, before QA ever sees the change, as a normal second set of eyes on the approach -- not a personal judgment, and it's completely normal for a reviewer to send work back before it's allowed to merge. The answer should use the STAR structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result), with Action describing reading the specific feedback carefully, asking a clarifying question if the reasoning wasn't obvious rather than assuming or arguing, making the requested change (or explaining a respectful disagreement if there was a good reason), and re-requesting review. Result should state the concrete outcome -- the change was approved and merged, and ideally what was learned or changed going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story rather than describe my attitude toward feedback in general. Situation: on my capstone's SSIS package, a reviewer flagged that my Lookup transformation had no error output configured, so a non-matching row would silently fail the whole package instead of being handled. Task: I needed to understand why that mattered and fix it properly, not just make the comment go away. Action: I asked the reviewer to walk me through what would actually happen with a non-matching row, since I hadn't considered it, then I configured the error output to redirect those rows to a dedicated log table instead of failing the package, and re-requested review with a short note explaining what I'd changed and why. Result: it was approved on the second pass, and I started checking every Lookup's error output by default on everything I built after that, which is the kind of habit a good review catches before it becomes a real production incident.
commonMistakes: Taking review feedback personally instead of treating it as a normal part of the Dev stage
Making the requested change without understanding why it was requested
Arguing defensively instead of asking a clarifying question when the reasoning isn't clear
Describing review feedback in general terms instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Code/report review happens inside the Dev stage, before QA -- it's a normal second set of eyes, not a personal judgment
Read specific feedback carefully; ask a clarifying question if the reasoning isn't obvious
Make the change (or explain a respectful disagreement), then re-request review
Use STAR and state the concrete Result -- what happened after the change was made

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames review feedback as a normal part of the process, not a personal setback
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result
