questions.title: Explaining a planned failover test to a non-technical manager
questions.prompt: You need to run a scheduled failover drill on the production database's Availability Group to confirm the HA/DR plan actually works, which requires a brief connection interruption during business hours. How would you explain this to a non-technical manager who will ask 'why do we need to cause an outage on purpose?'
questions.modelAnswer: The explanation should connect directly to the manager's own risk tolerance rather than staying technical. The core point: a failover plan that has never actually been tested is a plan nobody can trust -- if a real failure happens and the failover doesn't work the way everyone assumed, that discovery happens during an actual, unplanned outage, at the worst possible time, instead of during a scheduled few minutes everyone was expecting. A good answer gives a concrete, bounded ask -- a specific short window, during the lowest-traffic part of the day, with an exact expected duration and a rollback plan if something doesn't go as expected -- rather than an open-ended 'sometime soon, might take a while.' It should also state what's being verified concretely (that the secondary replica actually takes over correctly and the application reconnects) so the manager understands this isn't disruption for its own sake.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say something like: 'I want to schedule a 5-minute failover test for Tuesday at 6 AM, before traffic picks up, so we can confirm our disaster recovery plan actually works before we ever need it for real. The alternative is finding out it doesn't work during an actual outage, which is a much worse time to learn that.' I'd lead with the business risk, not the technical mechanism -- I wouldn't open with 'Always On' or 'synchronous commit,' I'd open with the fact that an untested plan is really just a guess, and a scheduled few minutes we control is a much better time to find a gap than the middle of a real incident. I'd also have a specific rollback answer ready if they ask what happens if it doesn't go smoothly, since being able to answer that confidently is usually what actually gets the window approved.
commonMistakes: Being vague about the actual duration or timing instead of giving a specific, bounded window
Leading with technical detail (Always On, synchronous commit, quorum) instead of the business risk being addressed
Not having a rollback plan to describe if asked
Treating the manager's question as an obstacle instead of a reasonable one that deserves a clear answer
keyPoints: Connect the request to the manager's own risk (an untested plan can't be trusted), not abstract HA/DR theory
Give a specific, bounded window and duration, not an open-ended ask
State concretely what's being verified
Have a rollback plan ready if asked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Connects the explanation to business risk rather than pure technical detail
Gives a specific, bounded request (window, duration)
Describes what's being verified and a rollback plan

questions.title: Knowing when to escalate a production incident you can't yet solve
questions.prompt: In your first month as a junior DBA, you're paged because a production database's CPU is pegged and several applications are reporting timeouts. You have some ideas but you're not fully confident you've found the actual cause. How do you decide whether to keep investigating on your own or escalate, and how would you escalate without it looking like you can't do the job?
questions.modelAnswer: This tests judgment about risk and communication, not raw troubleshooting skill. The deciding factor shouldn't be ego (will escalating make me look bad) -- it should be the actual business impact and how much time has already passed: a production-wide incident actively affecting multiple applications has a low tolerance for a junior DBA quietly investigating alone for an extended period on a hunch. A reasonable approach is time-boxing the initial investigation (for example, a firm 10-15 minutes to check the obvious things -- active sessions, blocking, recent deployments, resource metrics) before deciding, rather than either escalating instantly with no information or sitting on it indefinitely. Escalating well means bringing a specific, organized status, not just 'I'm stuck' -- what's confirmed so far, what's been ruled out, and the specific help needed -- which reads as competent triage, not as an admission of failure. Continuing to investigate in parallel with the senior person, rather than just handing it off and disengaging, also matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give myself about 10 minutes to check the obvious stuff -- sp_WhoIsActive for blocking, whether anything deployed recently, and the resource metrics in Azure Monitor. If I don't have a clear answer by then and it's still actively affecting production, I'd message the on-call senior DBA with exactly what I've checked, what I've ruled out, and what I'm leaning toward, and ask them to jump in rather than disappearing to keep digging alone. I'd remind myself that the decision to escalate isn't about whether it makes me look capable -- it's about how many applications are timing out right now and how long that's already been going on. Bringing a specific status instead of just 'it's broken, help' is what actually makes that escalation read as good triage instead of giving up.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck alone for too long out of fear that escalating looks like failure
Escalating immediately with zero information gathered, forcing the senior person to start from scratch
Escalating vaguely ('it's broken, help') instead of with a specific status and ask
Disengaging entirely after escalating instead of continuing to help in parallel
keyPoints: Decide to escalate based on business impact and time elapsed, not fear of looking incompetent
Time-box the initial solo investigation rather than going indefinitely or escalating instantly
Escalate with a specific status -- confirmed, ruled out, and the specific ask -- not just 'I'm stuck'
Stay engaged and helping after escalating, don't just hand off and disappear

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the escalation decision around impact/time, not ego
Describes a reasonable time-boxed investigation approach
Describes escalating with a specific, organized status
